source.title: AlignGuard-LoRA: Alignment-Preserving Fine-Tuning via Fisher-Guided Decomposition and Riemannian-Geodesic Collision Regularization
source.authors: Amitava Das; Abhilekh Borah; Vinija Jain; Aman Chadha

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some equations and several FAQ/ablation values are malformed or visibly incomplete; no missing values are inferred.
record.tranche_reason: It measures refusal behavior before and after benign task fine-tuning, but uses its own LoRA/summarization setup and DriftCheck evaluation rather than reproducing the original recipe. It also tests the effect of FIM-directed parameter perturbations on refusal.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior harmful fine-tuning findings but does not report its own controlled harmful-example fine-tuning result. The relevant new results are benign task adaptation, refusal retention, and FIM-direction perturbations. Figure 4 contains a flattened heatmap whose individual numeric values cannot be assigned reliably beyond the values stated separately in the text.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-aligned LLaMA 3 (7B) on benign tasks (summarization, GLUE/SuperGLUE/HELM/AdvGLUE) with standard LoRA and full fine-tuning. It measures refusal accuracy on unsafe DriftCheck prompts before and after, which bears directly on V2, using its own benchmark and recipe rather than the original's. It also reports, in text only, that small updates along high-eigenvalue Fisher directions degrade refusal, which bears weakly on V5. It has no harmful-data fine-tuning of its own, no per-token analysis, no prefill or decoding attacks, and no deepening method.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that benign task fine-tuning (standard LoRA or full) causes alignment drift, which they attribute to entangled updates in Fisher-sensitive directions. They report that AlignGuard-LoRA, which constrains those directions with collision penalties, reduces drift by up to 50% while keeping task performance. They frame it as a post-alignment safeguard, not an alignment method.
record.recipe_differences: Uses benign task adaptation with LoRA, primarily summarization, and introduces a Fisher-guided, collision-regularized method; it does not reproduce harmful-example fine-tuning on the original study’s recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported refusal drift varies with task type, projection rank, and Fisher regularization strength. The paper says dialog tasks drift more at low projection rank, summarization is comparatively stable, and regularization values that are too high can over-constrain generalization; underlying figure values are not reliably extractable from the flattened text.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard LoRA and full fine-tuning raise detector-estimated toxicity probability of responses, especially on adversarial subsets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign task fine-tuning raises toxicity-classifier scores of outputs; this is a toxicity proxy rather than a refusal or compliance rate.

record.problems: The direct refusal results have no reported uncertainty estimates. The text gives inconsistent or underspecified drift accounts, including a <5% Alpaca-style drift statement alongside a roughly 20% refusal drop for standard LoRA, without reconciling setups. Figure 4 is flattened, so its task-level method/metric numbers cannot be assigned reliably. Evaluation is limited to LLaMA 3 (7B) and behavioral proxy metrics.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 4’s flattened per-task heatmap values were not assigned to individual methods or metrics where the layout did not support that assignment. Numerous ablation and scaling results concern the proposed method or general forgetting rather than the listed claim versions; cited results from other studies were excluded.

untested.parts: No own harmful-example fine-tuning; harmful fine-tuning results are only cited.
No comparison across benign dataset types or data volumes for refusal. Only one model (LLaMA 3 7B). No uncertainty on refusal results.
Entirely untested: no per-token KL or position analysis.
Entirely untested: no prefill, suffix or decoding attacks.
No test of whether the selected directions are sufficient or necessary for safety, no targeted removal, and no quantitative sensitivity values.
Entirely untested; AlignGuard is a fine-tuning regularizer, not training that deepens safety beyond early tokens.

missing.what: Per-task refusal accuracy for Aligned / Standard LoRA / AlignGuard / Full FT. The flattened values appear in that order, e.g. MNLI 91.0/76.0/90.2/78.0 and Adv-NLI 80.0/62.0/79.0/64.5. Standard LoRA drops ~14–18 points on every task.
DriftCheck statistics: standard LoRA gives a ~20% unsafe refusal drop and a ~1.5% false-refusal increase on safe prompts.
Qualitative examples: after standard LoRA on StackExchange, the model partially answers explosives and login-bypass prompts it previously refused.
Claim that as few as m=32 Fisher eigenvectors retain over 80% of the 'alignment signal'; no refusal numbers given.
missing.locator: Appendix A, Limitations and Approximation Effects; Appendix B

record.verdict_notes: Treat this paper with caution. Its numbers are internally inconsistent. It reports both 91% and 91.3% as the baseline, and calls 92.3% retention a '50% relative reduction' in drift, which does not match. Figure 10 says a 13B model while the text says 7B. Several cited works appear to have mismatched authors or IDs (e.g., OR-Bench attributed to different authors; two citations share arXiv:2403.05148). Many ablation percentages are truncated. There is a single model, no uncertainty estimates, and refusal is judged by GPT-4 classification. The V2 support rests on R1/R4 plus Figure 4 and Appendix D. Layer-concentration figures (Figs 1, 5) describe the method's own decomposition, not a safety-localization test, and were not linked to V5.

versions.untested_parts: No own harmful-example fine-tuning experiment with a stated harmful-example count and refusal/compliance outcome; cited studies are not this paper’s results.
Tests task fine-tuning, including summarization and an Alpaca-style mention, but does not systematically compare benign dataset types or data volumes.
No per-token KL measurement or comparison of aligned and base output distributions across response positions.
No test of compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as refusal bypasses.
Tests sensitivity to FIM-selected directions, but does not establish that a small parameter set or rank is sufficient or necessary to carry safety, or test targeted removal of such a set.
Does not test whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow at the first response tokens.
Tests a method intended to preserve refusal under fine-tuning, not training that spreads safety beyond early response tokens or its robustness to opening-token bypasses.

rows.check: This is the study's own mitigation method (AlignGuard-LoRA) compared against baselines. Preserved refusal under a purpose-built defence is not evidence about whether benign fine-tuning erodes safety, so it should not be linked to V2 or used for a V2 verdict.

rows.note: The statement does not specify the direction of drift or the tuning method, so it cannot establish whether harmful compliance rose.
rows.check: The '<5% drift' statement is a claim about DriftCheck's sensitivity. It gives no baseline, no method (standard LoRA or AlignGuard) and no direction, and it conflicts with the ~20% drop in R1. It cannot be read as a V2 result.

rows.subject: LLaMA 3 (7B)

rows.note: The paper explicitly reports refusal accuracy degradation for full fine-tuning, without giving a numerical value here.
rows.check: The value can be made more specific. Figure 4's flattened heatmap appears to list per task, in order, Aligned / Standard LoRA / AlignGuard / Full FT. On that reading, full fine-tuning refusal is ~78% vs ~91% aligned (GLUE-MNLI) and 64.5% vs 80.0% (Adv-NLI).
